transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been going on that brought you here today?

Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. I, um, I guess I’m here because... well, it’s just getting to be too much. What brings me in is that I feel like I just can’t settle in my own body anymore. It’s this constant, buzzing sort of feeling, like a motor running right under my skin, and it’s especially bad when I’m supposed to just sit quietly. You know, like when I have to handle the paperwork for the house, or when my husband wants to sit down and go over our shared household plans, like the budget or the kids' schedules. 

I try to sit there at the dining room table with him, and he’s got his spreadsheets open, and I just... I can’t. My legs start bouncing, and I feel this physical need to just get up and do something else. I’ll start rearranging the salt and pepper shakers, or I’ll remember a load of laundry I need to switch, and I just have to get up. He gets so frustrated with me, and I get frustrated with myself, because I’m 41 years old, I have a degree, I should be able to just sit and look at a piece of paper for twenty minutes without feeling like I’m going to crawl out of my skin. But it’s just... it’s like my body is rejecting the idea of being still. It’s exhausting, honestly, just trying to force myself to stay in one place when every nerve is telling me to move.
Do you also feel this same sense of restlessness or need to move in other situations, like when you're waiting in line, watching TV, or trying to relax in the evening?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. The evenings are actually... well, they might even be worse in some ways because that's when you're supposed to be relaxing, right? Like, the whole house is finally quiet, the kids are in bed, and it’s just that time you're supposed to decompress. 

Take my husband, for example. He just wants to unwind. He’ll sit in his chair with a book, and I really, truly want to do the exact same thing. I’ll go all out—I’ll make a cup of chamomile tea, I’ll get my favorite throw blanket, I’ll pick out a novel from this giant stack I have by the bed, and I’ll sit right beside him on the sofa. I tell myself, okay, this is it, this is going to be a nice, quiet evening reading together. Just the two of us. 

But then... I don't know, it’s like the silence itself makes me antsy. I’ll read maybe half a page, and then I’ll suddenly remember I need to check if I actually started the dishwasher. So I get up. Then I come back and sit down. Then, without even realizing I'm doing it, I'll start humming. Just some random commercial jingle that's been stuck in my head all afternoon. Or I'll just start talking. I’ll completely interrupt his reading to tell him about an email I got from the PTA, or a random thought I had about reorganizing the pantry, or just... anything, really. 

And if I'm not talking or humming, I'm shifting my weight, or I'm getting up again to adjust the thermostat because suddenly the room feels too warm, and then getting up a third time to find a coaster for my tea. It’s just this endless stream of getting up for little things. And before I know it, I’m making enough noise and commotion that it completely stops being peaceful. He'll just sigh and put his bookmark in, and I feel so incredibly guilty because I wanted a quiet evening just as much as he did! I really did! But I just end up ruining it because sitting there in the quiet feels almost physically impossible after about five minutes.

Do you find it hard to focus or concentrate on tasks, even when you’re not physically restless—like when you’re reading, listening to someone talk, or trying to follow through on something you’ve started?

Yes, oh my gosh, yes. It’s not just the physical moving around, which is what makes it so confusing sometimes. Because even if I do manage to force my body to sit completely still, my brain is just... it's not cooperating at all. 

Like, I can sit down with a planning email—say, one of those really long messages from the school PTA about the spring fundraiser, or an email from my husband about our car insurance policy—and I will start out completely fine. I'll open it up, I'll read the first few lines, and I'm right there, you know? I'm engaged. But then, just a few minutes later, I’ll suddenly realize I’ve been staring at the exact same paragraph for I don't know how long, and absolutely none of it went in. My eyes are physically moving across the screen, I'm looking at the letters, but it’s like the words are just empty shapes. 

And it’s the exact same thing with reading for pleasure, which breaks my heart because I used to love reading. Like those novels I was telling you about, the ones in that giant stack by my bed? If I actually manage to stay on the sofa next to my husband and open one up, I’ll start a new chapter and think, okay, I’m reading, I’m doing it, I'm relaxing. But by the time I get to the bottom of the page, I have literally no idea what just happened in the story. I couldn't tell you if the main character walked into a room or if they fell off a cliff. I couldn't tell you a single thing I just read. 

So then I have to go back up to the top of the page and start all over again. And sometimes I'll do that three or four times! I'll just be staring at that same paragraph again and again, and my brain is just... it's a million miles away, thinking about grocery lists or a conversation I had with my sister three years ago, or wondering if I need to buy new filters for the vacuum. It’s incredibly frustrating because I genuinely want to read the book, and I really, really need to know what’s in those planning emails so I don't drop the ball on my kids' schedules, but it’s like there’s this total disconnect between my eyes and my brain the second I try to actually sustain my focus on something for more than a minute or two. It's like my attention just evaporates.
